faq.a: They block conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, raising the testosterone‑to‑DHT ratio and allowing more aromatisation to estrogen.
Pain is common in early puberty or acute hormonal shifts but many adult cases are painless.
For Grade III, persistent after 12 months of medical therapy, or when the mass causes significant psychosocial distress.

exam: A 17‑year‑old male presents with tender breast tissue for 2 months. What history points differentiate physiological puberty from pathology? — Look for drug use, liver disease, rapid unilateral growth, and systemic symptoms.

A patient on spironolactone develops bilateral gynecomastia. What is the next step? — Stop spironolactone, switch to a potassium‑sparing agent without anti‑androgen effect, and monitor for regression.
How does chronic hepatitis B lead to gynecomastia? — Liver dysfunction reduces sex‑hormone‑binding globulin clearance, increasing free estrogen.

You have a unilateral hard breast mass in a 45‑year‑old man with normal hormone levels. What is your priority investigation? — Ultrasound to differentiate gynecomastia from carcinoma; if suspicious, arrange core biopsy.

Explain why tamoxifen is used in refractory gynecomastia and why aromatase inhibitors are avoided in men with liver disease. — Tamoxifen blocks estrogen receptors in breast tissue; aromatase inhibitors can worsen hepatic dysfunction and are less effective when estrogen is already high.

A HIV‑positive man on efavirenz presents with gynecomastia. What is the likely mechanism and management? — Efavirenz induces hepatic enzymes increasing estrogen; consider switching ART and treat HIV; monitor breast tissue.
What red‑flag signs would prompt urgent referral to surgery? — Rapidly enlarging hard mass, skin ulceration, nipple retraction, or suspicion of malignancy.

During a ward round, a patient with cirrhosis has gynecomastia, spider naevi, and ascites. How does this affect your overall management plan? — Prioritise liver disease optimisation (diuretics, antiviral therapy), counsel on alcohol abstinence, and address gynecomastia after hepatic stability.
ai.title: Gynecomastia
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Gynecomastia is benign male breast enlargement due to an increased estrogen‑to‑androgen ratio. Recognise the common causes in low‑resource settings, stage severity, and manage the underlying condition before considering surgery.

b: Firm, rubbery disc‑shaped tissue under the nipple‑areolar complex
Distinguish from pseudogynecomastia (fat deposition) by pinch test
sections.p: A palpable, symmetric or unilateral enlargement of male breast tissue beneath the areola, confirmed by physical exam and, when needed, ultrasound to exclude lipoma or tumour.

b: Grade I: mild enlargement, no skin redundancy
Grade II: moderate enlargement, some skin stretch
Grade III: marked enlargement, skin excess, possible ptosis
sections.p: Use the Rohrlich classification (Grade I–III) based on size and skin changes; higher grades guide need for surgical referral.

b: Physiological puberty, ageing, obesity
Drugs: spironolactone, cimetidine, anti‑androgens, 5α‑reductase inhibitors (finasteride)
Liver disease (cirrhosis, hepatitis B), renal failure, hyperthyroidism
Infections: HIV, TB (especially with rifampicin), schistosomiasis (hepatic fibrosis)
Herbal remedies containing phyto‑estrogens
sections.p: Group aetiologies into physiological, drug‑induced, endocrine, and systemic diseases common in East Africa.

b: Tenderness early in puberty
Bilateral involvement in 80% of cases
Associated jaundice, spider naevi, testicular atrophy if hepatic or endocrine cause
sections.p: Young men notice tender, firm tissue; older men may have painless enlargement. Look for associated signs of liver disease, hypogonadism, or medication use.
Select tests that answer a specific clinical question; if a test is unavailable, use clinical clues or refer.

t.b: Is androgen deficiency present? Low level supports hypogonadism or drug effect
Is estrogen excess? Elevated level suggests hepatic failure or aromatase excess

t.a: Liver function tests (ALT, AST, bilirubin, albumin)
t.b: Is there hepatic dysfunction? Abnormal results point to cirrhosis or hepatitis
Is hyperthyroidism contributing? Suppressed TSH with high free T4 supports it
Is the mass solid (gynecomastia) or fatty/pseudogynecomastia? Guides need for biopsy
Is HIV infection present? Positive test may explain endocrine disruption

b: Unilateral hard mass, skin ulceration, nipple retraction
Rapid growth >6 weeks, weight loss, night sweats
Severe liver failure (ascites, encephalopathy) or uncontrolled hyperthyroidism
sections.p: Identify features that suggest malignancy or serious systemic disease.

b: Stop offending drugs; switch to alternatives without estrogenic activity
Treat liver disease: antiviral therapy for hepatitis B, abstinence from alcohol, nutrition support
Manage HIV with ART; control TB with appropriate regimen
Weight reduction and exercise for obesity‑related cases
Refer Grade III or refractory cases for subcutaneous mastectomy
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; symptomatic measures follow. Surgery is reserved for persistent high‑grade cases.

b: Repeat clinical exam and hormone panel
Screen for recurrence if drug re‑started
Counsel on avoiding herbal supplements with phyto‑estrogens
sections.p: Re‑evaluate at 3‑6 months after addressing the cause; monitor hormone levels and liver function. Educate on medication side‑effects and healthy weight.

b: Pseudogynecomastia – excess adipose tissue, no firm disc, improves with weight loss
Male breast carcinoma – hard, irregular, often unilateral, may have axillary nodes
sections.p: Distinguish true glandular gynecomastia from other breast enlargements.

b: Normal testosterone in early hypogonadism; repeat after fasting
Mildly elevated estradiol may be within assay variability; correlate clinically
Ultrasound may miss small carcinoma; persistent suspicion warrants biopsy
sections.p: Be aware of false‑negative or misleading investigations.
